resources.string: Selects which API login credentials the login flow requests. Example: use a supported combined login rather than manually pasting tokens when diagnosing missing access.
Application identifier used for the Helix login flow. Example: change only when configuring your own registered Twitch application; it must match your redirect configuration.
Return URL for the Helix login flow. Example: a custom registered client must use its matching redirect; leave the working default for normal sign-in.
Application identifier used for GQL requests. Example: change only to diagnose a compatible authentication setup; a client ID alone does not log you in.
Numeric Twitch ID for the current login. Example: inspect only when repairing a login setup; use the account menu for normal account changes.
Twitch login for the current account. Example: use normal sign-in to populate it; editing this alone does not switch saved accounts safely.
Credential used for Helix requests. Example: replace only during deliberate login repair. Treat it like a password; its value is not shown in settings summaries or search.
Credential used for GQL requests. Example: use normal sign-in to obtain it; manually change only for login repair. Its value is not shown in summaries or search.
Web-session credential used by supported Twitch actions. Example: reauthenticate normally if access expires. Keep it private; its value is not shown in summaries or search.
Checks saved credentials when the app starts. Example: leave on to detect an expired login instead of discovering it during an account action.

Minimum loading buffer in milliseconds; 15000 means 15 seconds. Example: raise it for steadier loading on a variable connection. This is a loading threshold, not a promised live delay. Reopen playback after changes.

Upper loading-buffer target in milliseconds; 50000 means 50 seconds. Example: allow more content ahead for VODs on an uneven connection. Keep at least the minimum buffer. Reopen playback after changes.
Buffered time required to start or resume after seeking, in milliseconds. Example: 2000 means 2 seconds. Low-delay mode uses its own live startup threshold. Reopen playback after changes.

Buffered time required to restart after a stall, in milliseconds. Example: increase it if playback repeatedly stops immediately after recovering. Low-delay mode overrides this for live streams. Reopen playback after changes.
Slowest automatic live speed; blank uses the player default. Example: 0.97 permits slight slowing to rebuild buffer. Low-delay mode uses its own range. Reopen the stream after changes.
Fastest automatic live catch-up speed; blank uses the player default. Example: 1.08 permits slight speeding up when behind. Low-delay mode uses its own range. Reopen the stream after changes.

Requested distance behind the live edge in milliseconds; 2000 means 2 seconds. Example: increase it for more headroom on weak Wi-Fi. Playlist/network limits still apply; low-delay mode overrides it. Reopen the stream after changes.
Makes chat usernames bold. Example: distinguish the sender from the message in fast chat.
Assigns a color when a user has not chosen one. Example: make otherwise identical-looking names easier to follow.
Adjusts username colors for contrast with the app theme. Example: keep dark names readable on a dark background.
Adds a time beside chat messages. Example: see when an earlier message arrived while reading back.
Chooses how message times are written when timestamps are enabled. Example: use a 24-hour format if you prefer it.
Selects the image loader used by chat. Example: try the alternate loader when troubleshooting missing emotes; keep the working default otherwise.
Requests WebP emote images where supported. Example: leave on for compatible providers, or turn off if your device fails to display them.
Chooses emote image resolution. Example: use higher quality for large emotes or lower quality to reduce image data.
Scales chat text, emotes and badges together; 100 is normal size. Example: increase this for an overall larger chat, then fine-tune individual sizes below.
Base chat text size before the overall size modifier. Example: increase just the message text without choosing a larger base emote size.
Base emote size before the overall size modifier. Example: enlarge emotes while leaving the message text smaller.
Base badge size before the overall size modifier. Example: shrink badges if they crowd usernames.
Displays GIF attachments in chat when supplied. Example: turn off if moving GIFs are distracting; animated emotes have a separate switch.
Base size of GIF messages. Example: reduce it if GIFs take too much chat space.
Chat\'s share of the screen in landscape; a larger value gives chat more room. Example: widen it for long messages at the cost of video space.
Maximum messages retained in the chat list. Example: lower it on a memory-limited phone, or raise it to read farther back.
Loads available messages from before you joined. Example: catch up on the conversation; history depends on the configured service.
Service used to load earlier chat messages; $channel becomes the channel login. Example: change only when using a compatible history service.
Maximum earlier messages requested when joining, separate from the retained-message limit. Example: load 100 older messages but keep 600 messages during viewing.
Translates chat messages using on-device language models. Example: read another language in your selected target language; model downloads need a connection.
Manage the downloaded translation models. Example: remove a language model you no longer use to free storage; this does not change stream filters.
Language to translate messages into. Example: select English to read supported chat languages in English; this is separate from the app menu language.
Keeps the chat connection when playback moves to the background. Example: maintain chat-related events while listening; turning it off can reduce background work.
Uses a WebSocket connection for IRC chat instead of a regular socket. Example: try the other transport if a network blocks chat connections.
Encrypts the IRC chat connection. Example: leave on for normal use; disabling is a troubleshooting option for compatible connections.
Connects to channel events such as points, raids, polls and predictions. Example: leave on for bonus-point events; individual event switches below select what is used or shown.
Claims available bonus chests while the active account is watching and events are available. Example: collect a periodic bonus without tapping. This does not spend points on rewards.
Shows a chat notice for received points events. Example: see when a bonus arrives; this does not enable background live-channel notifications.
Displays raid information received in chat. Example: see where a creator is sending viewers; automatic stream switching is separate.
Opens the destination stream when a raid event is received. Example: turn off if you want to stay on the original channel.
Displays received channel poll events. Example: follow a creator\'s current poll when the event connection supplies it.
Displays received channel prediction events. Example: see prediction information when available; this switch does not automatically spend points.
Shows supported 7TV decorative username paints. Example: turn off if elaborate name colors make chat hard to read.
Shows supported 7TV user badges. Example: hide them to reduce decoration beside names.
Loads supported 7TV personal emotes. Example: show a viewer\'s own available emotes, in addition to channel emotes.
Updates 7TV emotes when the channel changes its set. Example: see a newly added emote without reopening the stream.
Loads 7TV emotes. Example: enable if chat uses emote codes from 7TV instead of Twitch alone.
Loads BetterTTV emotes. Example: enable to display BTTV codes as images.
Loads FrankerFaceZ emotes. Example: enable for a channel using FFZ emote codes.
Displays subscription and similar user notices. Example: turn off to reduce event messages among normal chat.
Shows a notice when a single message is deleted. Example: see that a moderator removed a message; this controls event notices, not moderation permissions.
Shows timeout and ban notices received from chat. Example: see when moderation acts on a user; this does not give your account moderation privileges.
Controls emphasis on first-time chat and text reward redemptions. Example: show a label and background, background only, or display them as normal messages.
Animates supported emotes. Example: turn off moving emotes if you prefer a quieter chat; GIF messages are controlled separately.
Allows overlay emotes to combine with neighboring emotes. Example: display a hat overlay on a face instead of as a separate image.
Renders emote codes in system messages. Example: show an emote inside a subscription notice rather than plain text.
Turns off chat display/connection behavior. Example: use for video-only viewing; background chat and event features depend on a working chat session.
Adds a full IRC-message copy option for chat diagnostics. Example: inspect an event format when troubleshooting; copied messages can contain personal information.
Uses API requests for supported chat commands. Example: diagnose a command that fails through the chat connection.
Sends messages through the API instead of the IRC path where supported. Example: try for a specific send failure; this still uses the active account.
Shows extra connection information for troubleshooting. Example: investigate a chat disconnect; turn off when you no longer need the extra notices.
Selects the playback engine. Example: keep ExoPlayer for HexStream\'s low-delay behavior; try another engine only to diagnose a playback issue.
Uses the alternate EventSub chat path. Example: test a specific chat compatibility issue; this is separate from the normal IRC transport settings.
Adds playlist metadata to player diagnostics. Example: inspect a playback format problem; it does not control Twitch stream-tag filtering.
Includes an available Twitch integrity credential in supported requests. Example: use when diagnosing requests rejected by Twitch; this does not guarantee access.
Uses the embedded browser to obtain integrity information. Example: use for a compatible login-repair flow when integrity is needed.
Captures additional GQL headers during the supported browser flow. Example: use only for authentication troubleshooting; header values may be sensitive.
Advanced manually configured GQL request headers. Example: edit only to repair a known request issue. Treat them as private; values are not shown in summaries or search.
Runs the integrity acquisition flow now. Example: refresh an expired integrity credential when troubleshooting rejected requests.
Saves supported video downloads as a single file instead of separate playlist segments. Example: use for a file you want to play outside the app.
Restricts download jobs to Wi-Fi. Example: avoid using your mobile-data allowance; this does not restrict normal streaming playback.
Number of download jobs allowed at the same time. Example: lower it if several VOD downloads compete with playback; threads per job are separate.
Number of video chunks downloaded concurrently within a job. Example: reduce it on a slow connection; this is different from the number of simultaneous downloads.
Seconds between checks for new recording segments while a stream is live. Example: 2 checks often; a longer interval makes fewer requests. This does not set playback delay.
Seconds between checks for a stream to go live during a recording job. Example: 10 checks roughly every ten seconds; this is separate from notification polling.
Minutes a recording job waits for its stream to start. Example: 120 permits a two-hour wait; this does not control player startup buffering.
Minutes a recording job waits for another stream after one ends. Example: 15 can catch a quick restart before the job stops waiting.
Scans the app download folders for existing video and playlist files. Example: restore download-list entries after recovering files; it does not browse arbitrary phone folders.
Time allowed for a proxy request before failure handling, in milliseconds. Example: 3000 means 3 seconds; increase for a slow but working endpoint, lower for quicker failover.
Switches playlist variants during ads on direct playback. Example: try if ads interrupt a direct stream. Playback URL and HTTP proxy modes take priority, so this is unused while either is selected.
Set the platform/player variants tried for ad-time playlist swaps. Example: reorder variants when troubleshooting video swap on a direct connection.
Hides the player picture during detected ads. Example: avoid seeing an ad segment; this does not skip its duration or guarantee ad removal.
Comma-separated video codecs to request in preference order. Example: av1,h265,h264 allows newer formats with H.264 as a fallback; actual options depend on the stream and device.
Includes the active account login in live access requests. Example: allow Twitch to recognize a subscription for a subscriber-only stream; this does not grant access you do not have.
Includes the active account login in VOD access requests. Example: let Twitch check your subscription for a restricted recording; it does not bypass access rules.
Shows the Minimize shortcut on the video controls. Example: continue browsing with the video in the in-app mini-player. Menu visibility is configured separately.
Shows the Download shortcut on the video controls. Example: save available content from the current video. Menu visibility is configured separately.
Shows the Follow shortcut on the video controls. Example: follow the current channel without leaving the player. Menu visibility is configured separately.
Shows the Sleep timer shortcut on the video controls. Example: stop playback after a chosen time. Menu visibility is configured separately.
Uses the Material time-selection dialog for the sleep timer. Example: choose it if you prefer a clock-style picker.
Locks the screen when the sleep timer finishes; requires device-admin permission. Example: let the phone lock after falling asleep to a stream.
Opens Android device-admin controls used by the sleep-timer lock feature. Example: revoke that permission when you stop using automatic locking.
Shows the Aspect ratio shortcut on the video controls. Example: adjust how a video fits the screen. Menu visibility is configured separately.
Shows the Playback speed shortcut on the video controls. Example: watch a recorded video faster or slower. Menu visibility is configured separately.
Playback speeds offered by the speed picker, one number per line. Example: 1.0 is normal and 1.5 is one-and-a-half speed; this is separate from automatic live catch-up.
Shows the Quality shortcut on the video controls. Example: reduce resolution when a connection struggles. Menu visibility is configured separately.
Shows the Player menu shortcut on the video controls. Example: reach less-used actions without filling the video with buttons. Menu visibility is configured separately.
Choose actions inside the player menu. Example: keep Quality here while hiding its separate on-video button.
Shows the Chapters shortcut on the video controls. Example: jump to another game segment in a supported VOD. Menu visibility is configured separately.
Shows the Restart player shortcut on the video controls. Example: reload playback if it gets stuck. Menu visibility is configured separately.
Shows the Seek to live shortcut on the video controls. Example: jump to the newest available live position after pausing. Menu visibility is configured separately.
Shows the Volume shortcut on the video controls. Example: adjust sound using a button instead of a swipe. Menu visibility is configured separately.
Shows the Audio compressor shortcut on the video controls. Example: reduce the difference between quiet and loud audio on supported devices. Menu visibility is configured separately.
Shows the Audio only shortcut on the video controls. Example: listen without displaying the video. Menu visibility is configured separately.
Shows the Subtitles shortcut on the video controls. Example: toggle captions when the source supplies them. Menu visibility is configured separately.
Shows the Chat input shortcut on the video controls. Example: show or hide the message composer. Menu visibility is configured separately.
Shows the Chat shortcut on the video controls. Example: show or hide the chat panel. Menu visibility is configured separately.
Shows the Fullscreen shortcut on the video controls. Example: expand the player to use more of the display. Menu visibility is configured separately.
Double-tapping the video shows or hides chat. Example: quickly get chat out of the way while watching.
Seconds to jump backward with the rewind control. Example: 10 replays the last ten seconds when that content is available.
Seconds to jump forward with the forward control. Example: 10 skips ten seconds in a VOD; it cannot go beyond available live content.
Shows the channel name on player controls. Example: keep it visible when frequently switching streams.
Shows the stream or video title on player controls. Example: hide it if a long title crowds the controls.
Shows the current game/category on player controls. Example: see what a creator is playing without leaving playback.
Shows how long the live stream has been running in the player. Example: distinguish a fresh stream from an all-day broadcast; directory uptime is separate.
Makes the player viewer count open the viewer list. Example: tap the count to inspect the supplied list; this is different from showing a viewer-list menu item.
Shows icons beside viewer count and uptime. Example: hide them for a less decorated player display.
Shows a pause control during live playback. Example: pause briefly, then use LIVE to catch up; pausing naturally puts you behind live.
Adds Quality to the player menu. Example: change resolution while keeping the separate quality button hidden. This does not enable its separate on-video button.
Adds Playback speed to the player menu. Example: adjust a VOD speed from the menu. This does not enable its separate on-video button.
Adds Viewer list to the player menu. Example: open the available viewer list without tapping the viewer count. This does not enable its separate on-video button.
Adds Chapters to the player menu. Example: jump between supported VOD game segments. This does not enable its separate on-video button.
Adds Download to the player menu. Example: save available content from the current video. This does not enable its separate on-video button.
Adds Bookmark to the player menu. Example: save a VOD position to return to later. This does not enable its separate on-video button.
Adds Share to the player menu. Example: copy or send the current Twitch link. This does not enable its separate on-video button.
Adds Find unlisted video to the player menu. Example: look for an available recording that is missing from the normal list. This does not enable its separate on-video button.
Adds Sleep timer to the player menu. Example: stop playback after a chosen time. This does not enable its separate on-video button.
Adds Aspect ratio to the player menu. Example: change how the picture fits the screen. This does not enable its separate on-video button.
Adds Volume to the player menu. Example: adjust sound without a standalone volume button. This does not enable its separate on-video button.
Adds Subtitles to the player menu. Example: toggle captions when the source provides them. This does not enable its separate on-video button.
Adds Restart player to the player menu. Example: reload a stream that has become stuck. This does not enable its separate on-video button.
Adds Chat input to the player menu. Example: show or hide the message composer. This does not enable its separate on-video button.
Adds Chat to the player menu. Example: show or hide the chat panel. This does not enable its separate on-video button.
Adds Reload emotes to the player menu. Example: refresh channel emotes after the creator changes the set. This does not enable its separate on-video button.
Adds Disconnect from chat to the player menu. Example: stop the current chat connection. This does not enable its separate on-video button.
Stops rendering the picture during background audio. Example: leave on when listening with the screen off; this does not itself switch to a smaller audio-only download.
Switches to an available audio-only stream in the background. Example: save bandwidth while listening; switching back can briefly reload the video.
Keeps sound playing after closing the floating PiP window with the screen awake. Example: turn off if closing that window should stop playback.
Keeps sound playing when locking the phone from PiP. Example: continue listening after turning off the screen; the non-PiP lock switch is separate.
Prevents normal screen timeout while the video is paused. Example: keep a paused frame visible while checking a game detail.
Lets another app interrupt playback when it requests audio focus. Example: pause HexStream when starting music elsewhere.
Pauses when headphones disconnect. Example: avoid unexpectedly sending stream audio through the phone speaker.
Shows the available live seek range in the media notification. Example: move within buffered live video without opening the app; it cannot seek beyond available content.
Quality to use when opening playback outside the cellular override. Example: choose a lower resolution to reduce data, or use the saved choice.
Quality to use on mobile data. Example: select a lower resolution here while keeping a higher default on Wi-Fi.
Moves video controls away from rounded display corners. Example: enable if a corner clips a button on your phone.
Lets the in-app minimized player move freely instead of staying constrained. Example: move it away from a card you want to tap.
Remembers where you stopped recorded videos. Example: resume a long VOD later; this does not freeze a live stream position.
Clears saved VOD resume positions. Example: use when you want watched videos to start over; it does not delete downloaded video files.
Swipe vertically on the left quarter of the video with controls hidden. Example: brighten a dark scene; drag the center to minimize as usual.
Swipe vertically on the right quarter of the video with controls hidden. Example: lower a loud stream; center and mini-player gestures still work.

Uses short live startup buffers and automatic catch-up in ExoPlayer. Example: leave on to stay near live; turn off if a weak connection repeatedly stalls. Overrides advanced live offset/speed and startup/rebuffer values. Reopen the stream after changing it.
Changes the app menus, not stream filtering or chat translation. Example: choose English for the interface while browsing streams in any language.
Lets content use the area around a camera notch. Example: turn this off if text or controls sit behind your camera cutout.
Checks followed channels for the active account only. Example: turn on live alerts here; individual channel alerts must also be enabled.
Colors, corner shapes and spacing. Example: pick a dark theme for watching at night.
Directory cards, tabs and browsing layout. Example: show more columns or hide thumbnails for a denser list.
Chat appearance, emotes, translation and bonus-point collection. Example: increase text size if chat is hard to read.
Shows a floating video when leaving the app on supported devices. Example: watch while checking another app; background audio has separate switches below.
Keeps audio playing after leaving the app with the screen awake, outside Picture-in-Picture. Example: listen while reading another app.
Keeps audio playing with the screen locked, outside Picture-in-Picture. Example: listen with the phone in your pocket; this is separate from awake-screen playback.
Playback defaults, background behavior, swipes and low delay. Example: adjust brightness with a swipe or change cellular quality.
Choose shortcuts shown on the video and their behavior. Example: hide a Quality button and keep the same action in the player menu instead.
Advanced ExoPlayer buffering and live timing. Example: allow more buffering on an unreliable connection; Low-delay live playback overrides some live settings.
Tries enabled playback URL presets in order, across all accounts. Example: enable for EU2 Luminous first, then the next working preset. Takes priority over HTTP proxies and video swap.
Edit, enable or reorder shared playback endpoints. Example: drag a working preset to the top; changing accounts keeps this list.
Routes selected playback requests through an HTTP host and port. Example: use a proxy you manage. Used only when playback URL proxies are off; separate from the preset URLs above.
Configure HTTP host, port, optional login and request types. Example: proxy playlist requests through your own server; these are not the Luminous/PerfProd URL presets.
Advanced proxy timeout, ad handling and access requests. Example: increase the timeout if a working proxy is slow to respond.
Advanced login and API configuration. Example: inspect this when diagnosing authentication trouble; normal account switching belongs in the account menu.
Selects the app networking backend. Example: try the other backend when diagnosing a connection problem; leave the current one if everything works.
Download storage behavior, Wi-Fi use and recording checks. Example: restrict downloads to Wi-Fi to save mobile data.
Checks the configured release feed now. Example: use this to look for a newer APK without waiting for a startup check.
Control update checks and how APKs open. Example: check weekly or download through your browser.

Writes the general preferences and app database to a folder you choose. Example: keep a copy before a reset. This is not a complete account-vault or global-filter/proxy backup; export filters separately.
Restores the preferences XML and database files from a backup. Example: select those files to recover supported app data; account sign-ins and separately exported global filters need their own setup.
HexStream by TripleSix, built on Xtra, with Unwanted Twitch inspiration and dependency credits. Example: open for version information and source links.
Advanced troubleshooting controls. Example: change a backend only when investigating a specific issue; leave working defaults alone.
Selects the app color theme when following the device theme is off. Example: choose a dark palette for night viewing.
Automatically switches between the two themes below using the device light/dark setting. Example: let Android\'s night schedule change HexStream too.
Theme used when Android dark mode is on and system following is enabled. Example: choose a dark or black palette for nighttime.
Theme used when Android dark mode is off and system following is enabled. Example: use a lighter palette during the day.
Changes card corner rounding. Example: choose square corners for a sharper directory layout.
Reduces space around interface content. Example: fit more browsing information on a small screen.
Uses a more compact text presentation. Example: fit more information in dense lists; leave off if readability matters more.
Adds separation to the top bar when content scrolls underneath. Example: keep the toolbar visually distinct in long settings lists.
Applies the theme color to the bottom navigation area. Example: make navigation match your chosen palette.
Uses Material 3 styling for supported controls and dialogs. Example: enable for the newer dialog appearance; disable if you prefer the older style.
Number of directory cards across with the phone upright. Example: choose one for large previews or more for a denser grid.
Number of cards across with the phone sideways. Example: add columns to use a wide screen more efficiently.
Choose a Twitch-account follow button, a local-only follow button or hide it. Example: use local follows to save channels in the app without following them on Twitch.
Enables a channel alert when you follow it. Example: turn off to follow silently. Live notifications must also be enabled, and only the active account is checked.
Choose whether startup opens Following. Example: go straight to your followed streams; the bottom-tab default and order are configured separately.
Show, reorder and choose a default bottom tab. Example: put Following first and hide a tab you rarely use.
Show, reorder and choose the default Following section. Example: open followed live streams before followed games.
Show, reorder and choose the default Saved section. Example: put bookmarks before downloads.
Show, reorder and choose the default channel section. Example: open a channel on Videos instead of Clips.
Show, reorder and choose the default game section. Example: keep live streams first and hide a section you do not use.
Show, reorder and choose the default search section. Example: put channel results ahead of clips.
Replaces stream preview cards with a more compact presentation in selected orientations. Example: hide previews when you want more rows visible at once.
Choose which name appears when a display name differs from the login. Example: show the login to recognize the same creator across name styling changes.
Uses circular profile pictures. Example: turn off if you prefer the full rectangular avatar.
Shortens large numbers. Example: show about 12K instead of a long viewer count.
Shows how long a stream has been live on directory cards. Example: spot a stream that just started; the player has a separate uptime display switch.
Shows supplied tags on directory cards. Example: read tags while browsing. Hiding the chips does not disable filtering of the full supplied tag list.
Shows how many channels are live in a game when supplied. Example: distinguish many small streams from a few large ones.
Uses swipeable sections within Following. Example: turn off if you prefer navigating its sections without the tab pager.
Uses swipeable sections within Saved. Example: switch between bookmarks and downloads with tabs.
Uses swipeable sections within Games. Example: switch between game lists with tabs.
Shows a shortcut back to the top of a scrolled list. Example: return quickly after browsing a large category; it does not refresh the snapshot.
Shows remaining time on bookmarked VODs. Example: find something short enough to finish before leaving.
Keeps searches in the app history. Example: turn off on a shared phone if you do not want new searches remembered.
Clears the saved search history. Example: remove earlier searches; turn off Store recent searches to stop saving new ones.
Release feed used to check for APK updates. Example: keep the official HexStream feed for this app; change only to a trusted compatible feed.
Checks for a newer version when opening the app, subject to the interval below. Example: enable for update notices without checking manually.
Minimum days between startup update checks. Example: 7 checks no more often than weekly; Check for updates still lets you check now.
Opens update downloads in your browser instead of the app installer flow. Example: use when you prefer choosing where an APK is saved.

Shared across all accounts. Enable the endpoints you want, then drag the handle to set the order. Playback tries enabled endpoints in order and uses the first working one. Example: move a reliable preset to the top; a status check alone does not prove a live stream will play.

HTTP host/port entries belong to the active account and are used when playback URL proxies are off. Enable entries and drag to set their order. Example: route selected requests through your own server. The shared Luminous/PerfProd presets are in Playback URL presets instead.

Direct-playback ad-time variants for this account. Enable entries and drag movable rows to choose the order; the fixed first row stays first. Example: put a working platform/player combination before other movable variants. Unused while either proxy mode is selected.
Enter a full playback endpoint URL. $channel becomes the Twitch login. Example: https://example.com/live/$channel. Use a service compatible with Twitch playback playlists.
Adds the app\'s playback query parameters. Example: leave off for a preset URL that already supplies all required options; enable only when your endpoint expects the extra parameters.
Proxy server hostname or IP, without a URL path. Example: proxy.example.com. Enter its listening port separately, such as 8080.
Optional credentials for the proxy server, not your Twitch login. Example: leave both empty if your proxy does not require authentication.
Routes playback-access requests through this HTTP proxy. Example: enable if your server must handle the request that obtains permission to play.
Routes the master playlist through this HTTP proxy. Example: use when the request listing available qualities needs that route.
Routes media-playlist requests through this HTTP proxy. Example: use when the changing list of video segments needs that route.
Listening port supplied by your proxy service. Example: 8080; enter only the number, not a URL.
Password for this proxy, if required. Example: leave empty for a proxy without authentication; do not put a Twitch password here.
Platform value sent for this variant. Example: web. Use a value supported by Twitch playback requests.
Player-type value sent for this variant. Example: site. Match it with a compatible platform; changing these is advanced troubleshooting.
